subject: anaesthesia
title: Local Anaesthetic Chemistry: Esters, Amides, pKa, and Onset of Action

steps.title: Ester versus Amide Chemical Classes
steps.tx: **Classification of ester and amide anaesthetics** divides local anaesthetics into two distinct metabolic families: esters (procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine, benzocaine, cocaine) contain an ester (-COO-) linkage, whereas amides (lignocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine, mepivacaine, etidocaine) contain an amide (-NHCO-) linkage. Amide molecules are recognized by having two letter 'i's in their spelling, while esters contain only one letter 'i'.

steps.title: Pseudocholinesterase Metabolism of Esters
steps.tx: **Plasma pseudocholinesterase ester clearance** breaks down amino-ester local anaesthetics rapidly within circulating blood via butyrylcholinesterase. This rapid hydrolysis prevents ester accumulation in the body, resulting in ultra-short elimination half-lives (under one minute for chloroprocaine), though patients with genetic pseudocholinesterase deficiency or organophosphate toxicity experience significantly slowed ester clearance.

steps.title: Para-Aminobenzoic Acid Allergic Reactions
steps.tx: **Para-aminobenzoic acid allergenicity** explains why ester local anaesthetics carry a substantially higher risk of true IgE-mediated anaphylactic reactions than amides. Enzymatic cleavage of procaine, tetracaine, and chloroprocaine liberates para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), a potent immunogenic hapten that sensitizes mast cells. In contrast, true allergic reactions to amino-amides are extraordinarily rare, almost universally triggered by methylparaben preservatives.

steps.title: Hepatic Cytochrome Clearance of Amides
steps.tx: **Hepatic clearance kinetics of amides** depend on hepatic blood flow and microsomal cytochrome P450 enzymes (specifically CYP1A2 and CYP3A4). Because amides possess intermediate-to-high hepatic extraction ratios, conditions that decrease hepatic perfusion (congestive heart failure, general anaesthesia, beta-adrenergic blockade) or impair microsomal enzyme function (cirrhosis) substantially prolong elimination half-lives, elevating systemic toxicity risk.

steps.title: pKa and Henderson-Hasselbalch Kinetics
steps.tx: **pKa governing anaesthetic onset velocity** represents the dissociation constant at which exactly 50 percent of the drug exists in the uncharged lipophilic base form (B) and 50 percent exists in the charged hydrophilic cation form (BH+). According to the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, anaesthetics with a pKa closest to physiological tissue pH (7.4) possess the largest fraction of uncharged base, driving rapid membrane diffusion and fast clinical onset.

steps.title: Acidosis and Infection Failure
steps.tx: **Local anaesthetic failure in infected tissues** occurs when acidic inflammatory exudate (tissue pH falling to 5.5 to 6.0 within an abscess) disrupts the Henderson-Hasselbalch equilibrium. Acidosis heavily ionizes the local anaesthetic into its charged cation form (BH+), leaving under one percent as uncharged lipophilic base (B), rendering molecules incapable of traversing the hydrophobic lipid axonal membrane to reach internal sodium channels.

steps.title: Sodium Bicarbonate Alkalinisation
steps.tx: **Alkalinisation using sodium bicarbonate** accelerates the onset of local anaesthesia and reduces injection pain. Adding 1 milliliter of 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate to 10 milliliters of 1 percent or 2 percent lignocaine elevates solution pH closer to 7.4, increasing the fraction of uncharged lipophilic base four-fold, accelerating neural onset while neutralizing acidic commercial hydrochloric acid vehicles.

steps.title: Lipid Solubility and Protein Binding
steps.tx: **Lipid solubility and protein binding metrics** govern anaesthetic potency and duration: lipid solubility (measured by the octanol-water partition coefficient) correlates directly with intrinsic anaesthetic potency, allowing lower drug concentrations to block nerve conduction. Plasma protein binding (primarily to alpha-1 acid glycoprotein) correlates with receptor attachment duration, determining the persistence of clinical anaesthesia.
